newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Boehler, VA Stahl face pinch.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Boehler, VA Stahl face pinch.

text.p: Austrian steel heavyweights VA Stahl and Boehler-Uddeholm, due to post first-half results next week, should continue to outperform Europe but will suffer a nasty blow to profits from recent tax changes, analysts said.
"The steel industry is seeing falling sales, falling volumes and falling profits," said Alan Coats, steel analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
He noted steel spot market prices had tumbled almost 20 percent and European production was down 8.5 percent this year, but said Austrian steel companies tended to be more robust.
"With VA Stahl we would expect a fall in sales and a fall in profit margins, but not as much as in the rest of the industry," he said.
He forecast a fall in net profit to around one billion schillings for the first half of 1996 from 1.69 billion for the same period last year.
Coats said VA Stahl's cost reduction programme in Linz and considerable business on contract were reasons for optimism, but said the trend would be downward in the second half.
Victoria Maxwell at James Capel in London agreed that the medium-term outlook was gloomy.

"VA Stahl have been protected by long term contracts which were signed when prices were at their peak, but the negotiations are coming around again and now prices are at a low which will mean next year's results will be even worse."

Austrian analyst Paul Severin at Creditanstalt-Bankverein also forecast a drop in the first six months but did not see the decline as a cause for concern as it included a deconsolidation from last year.

As for high-grade steelmaker Boehler-Uddeholm, Gerhard Auer, analyst at ICE Securities in London, said he saw first-half results in line with the year-ago period, but predicted there would similarly be a slide downwards in the second half.
"We would expect the sales figure to probably come down a bit and therefore the margins up a bit," he said, noting that growth in South East Asia would not be enough to compensate for the decline.

Analysts said both VA Stahl and Boehler would feel the pinch in profit growth in 1996 and 1997 as a result of government tax changes, which mean previously incurred losses will not be tax deductible for those years.
James Capel's Maxwell forecast a drop in VA Stahl's earnings per share to 59 schillings in 1996 from 106 schillings posted in 1995, and a further slide to 54 schillings in 1997.
"You've got to appreciate that 1996 and 1997 have been really impacted by the tax, but we've also got weakness at the operating level," she said, but added a pick-up was expected in 1998.
